claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has an intact native oxide scale.
Thermal cycling between room temperature and 800 °C in the presence of a salt deposit induces microcracks in the native oxide scale.
Thermal cycling promotes microcracking through differential thermal expansion between the oxide scale and the steel substrate.
Differential thermal expansion produces stress concentrations in the oxide scale and at the oxide/substrate interface.
Oxide-scale microcracks act as pathways for salt ingress.
Salt penetration through oxide-scale microcracks initiates localized corrosion.
Static high-temperature exposure promotes a more uniform, continuous, and adherent oxide layer than thermal cycling.
A uniform and adherent oxide layer impedes corrosion.
Thermally cycled samples will develop more extensive microcrack networks than statically exposed samples.
Thermally cycled samples will exhibit greater mass loss than statically exposed samples.
Thermally cycled samples will exhibit lower hardness than statically exposed samples.
Microcrack density will correlate strongly with corrosion degradation.
The proposed mechanism applies when thermal cycling generates significant differential-expansion stresses.
Stabilizing the oxide scale through alternative treatments may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
The proposed salt-ingress corrosion mechanism may not apply in the absence of a salt deposit.
Oxidation kinetics and scale-composition differences may independently affect degradation under different thermal regimes.
